S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S056.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
S056.description: Excessive anxiety and worry (expectant apprehension) occurring persistently about a number of events or activities.

subtypes.Chronic Worry: Worry occurs more days than not for at least 6 months.
subtypes.Generalized Worry: Worry is not confined to specific topics but spreads to various domains like work, school, family, and finances.
subtypes.Catastrophizing: Jumping to conclusions that minor mistakes or events will lead to irreversible disasters.
subtypes.Intolerance of Uncertainty: Unable to tolerate future uncertainty, trapped in 'what if' questions.

S057.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
S057.description: The subjective experience of finding it difficult to stop or control the worry.

subtypes.Failure to Control: Unable to regulate worry despite efforts to stop or distract oneself.
subtypes.Intrusive Worry: Worries suddenly intrude into the mind and interfere with focus while doing other tasks.
subtypes.Chaining of Worry: One worry triggers another in a chain reaction, escalating to catastrophic thoughts.

S058.name: Restlessness_Tension
S058.description: Restlessness, or feeling keyed up or on edge.

subtypes.Feeling Keyed Up: Feeling anxious and wound up like a spring, unable to stay still.
subtypes.Physical Tension: The entire body feels stiff and tense, unable to relax.
subtypes.Nervousness: Nerves are on edge, being startled easily by minor sounds or stimuli.

S059.name: Concentration_Difficulty
S059.description: Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank.

subtypes.Interference by Worry: Unable to focus on the task at hand because worries keep surfacing.
subtypes.Inability to Sustain Attention: Attention is scattered due to anxiety, making it hard to focus on one thing for long.
subtypes.Mind Going Blank: Suddenly the mind goes empty or white, and no thoughts occur.

symptom.disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains of life (e.g., work, health, finances, family) occurring more days than not for at least several months, typically 6 months or longer. The worry is experienced as difficult to control and is commonly accompanied by physical and cognitive symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, impaired concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, which cause clinically significant distress or functional impairment. The course is often chronic and fluctuating, with periods of exacerbation during psychosocial stress; onset can be gradual and is frequently recognized only after worry and associated tension begin to interfere with occupational, academic, or interpersonal functioning. It is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the breadth and pervasiveness of worry rather than discrete attacks (as in panic disorder) or circumscribed fears (as in specific phobia), and by the absence of primary obsessions or compulsions as in OCD.

patient.stressor: About nine months ago, Anabella was promoted to take on more complex support responsibilities, including being the primary bilingual point of contact for a major corporate client while also mentoring new hires and organizing a women‑in‑tech workshop series. What initially felt like an exciting opportunity gradually turned into a constant sense that she could never fully disconnect, as on‑call escalations, back‑to‑back tickets, and expectations to script new automation piled onto her existing community and creative commitments. She began spending longer hours triple‑checking configurations and email threads, skipping dance nights and hikes to keep up with work queues, which disrupted the balance between structure and spontaneity that usually kept her grounded. When her manager gently noted a drop in her responsiveness during meetings and she realized she was lying awake most nights running through hypothetical system failures and career missteps, she finally agreed with a friend’s suggestion to see a mental health professional.
patient.chief_complaint: “My mind just won’t shut off about work and everything else, and I can’t seem to turn the worrying off no matter what I do.”

patient.stressor: Terrell’s anxiety escalated over the past nine months after his wife returned to work full‑time following the birth of their second child, leaving him juggling demanding senior engineering duties, leadership of an Agile team, and increased responsibilities at home. His drive to outperform at work led him to accept a high‑visibility cloud migration project just as childcare logistics, financial planning for a larger house, and his parents’ emerging health issues all converged, leaving him feeling solely responsible for keeping everything running smoothly. He began turning routine family and work decisions into high‑stakes mental calculations, rereading code and project plans late into the night and second‑guessing his availability as a husband and father, which strained his relationship as he grew more irritable and withdrawn. The tipping point came when his wife confronted him about missing yet another family event because he was stuck reworking an already‑approved deployment, and he realized he was constantly tense and on edge around his family; at her urging, he agreed to seek psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I feel constantly wound up and on edge, like I can’t relax even when I’m just at home with my family.”

patient.stressor: Sunny’s difficulties became pronounced when her clinic announced a reorganization about nine months ago, hinting that front‑desk roles would be consolidated and that she might be expected to assume more office‑manager duties without a clear timeline or job description. At the same time, several long‑time coworkers left, and she found herself covering multiple schedules, learning new software, and trying to prove she could handle the expanded responsibilities she’d quietly hoped for, all while maintaining her art workshops, photography projects, and community volunteering. The uncertainty about her future role and income, combined with her tendency to over‑commit to evening classes and outreach events, left her feeling like she was constantly behind, and she started staying late at the office and bringing worries about minor scheduling errors home with her. When she noticed that she was rereading simple emails, losing track of conversations at the front desk, and spending her late‑night museum visits preoccupied with what might go wrong the next day, she confided in a colleague who recommended she speak with a mental health professional.
patient.chief_complaint: “Lately I can’t seem to focus at work—my mind keeps drifting back to everything that could go wrong with my job.”
